1:
Theophylact ties the saying to what precedes: the Pharisees were covetous and railed at Christ when he preached poverty, so he told them the parable of the rich man, and then, speaking to his disciples of those Pharisees, described them as men who caused division and laid obstacles in the divine way. Cyril of Alexandria opens his homily the same way, promising to supply what was still wanting to the parable of Lazarus. John Gill notes that several copies read that he said this to his disciples, and takes him to repeat what he had said before on another occasion. Charles Ellicott allows that the want of connection might justify treating the precepts as recorded for their own value, but suspects a dropped link, since the self-indulgent life of the parable was itself an offence that must needs come in the Christian Church as in the Jewish, and would still bring woe on the man through whom it came.

What the offences are is answered several ways. Cyril distinguishes two kinds, those which resist the glory of God — heresies and words spoken against the truth — and those which merely trip up a brother, such as strifes and slanders; the second is meant here, since the next verse turns at once to a brother who trespasses. Theophylact takes them more widely, as hindrances to preaching and to the truth of the kind the Pharisees raised. John Wesley is blunt that they come chiefly by Pharisees, men who trust in themselves that they are righteous and despise others. Matthew Henry divides the woe three ways: against persecutors who discourage the least of Christ’s little ones, against seducers who corrupt his truths, and against those who bear the Christian name and live scandalously.

Why the author is blamed for what must happen is sharper. Theophylact answers that necessity itself is born of free will, and that the Lord, seeing how men cling to evil, spoke only of the consequence of what is seen — as a physician watching an unwholesome diet may say it is impossible but such a man should be sick. Matthew Henry answers from providence, that God carries on his work even by these offences, yet it is no abatement of the offender’s guilt that they must come. Adam Clarke grounds the certainty in the corrupt heart, where men sin on despite all the influences of grace, so that justice must continue to punish; Albert Barnes says only that such is the state of things that it cannot but happen. A.T. Robertson resists the fatal sound of the English, the word meaning inadmissible rather than destined, and notes the positive form of the saying at Matthew 18:7. Chrysostom turns the threat into a comfort: from the punishment of the offender learn the reward of the man who saves, for had the salvation of one soul not been of such care to Christ he would never have threatened so heavily.

The millstone is a matter of custom and of grammar. John Lightfoot and Adam Clarke both show that a millstone about the neck was a common proverb, quoting the rabbinic question whether a man can study the law with a millstone about his neck, and both cite the comic poet’s line about plunging a man into the deep with a stone at his neck; Lightfoot adds the Talmudic distinction of ass-mill from hand-mill. A.T. Robertson notes that the verb rendered “it were better” is a commercial word meaning a thing pays its costs, and makes a point against the versions: the millstone clause is a first-class condition, stated as fulfilled, not the remote supposition the English implies. Charles Ellicott and John Wesley agree that the little ones are disciples or weak believers, Ellicott adding that they may be offended either way, tempted by the bad example or shaken by seeing the form of godliness without the power.
3:
Ambrose reads the command as a guard against despair: after the parable of the rich man, Christ added an order to forgive those who turn from their trespasses, lest any fail to be reclaimed through hopelessness. The block continues under a hand the scrape has not separated, answering the warning just given — offences must come, but it does not follow that you must perish if you are on your guard, any more than the sheep need perish when the wolf comes if the shepherd watches — and laying down a rule for the rebuke: neither a hard-wrung pardon nor a too easy forgiveness, neither an upbraiding that disheartens nor an overlooking that invites more, since friendly correction strikes shame into a man while quarrelsome accusation moves only indignation, and fear is a weak preserver of consistency where shame is an excellent master of duty.

Charles Ellicott finds the placing of “take heed to yourselves” remarkable, nothing answering to it in the parallel, and reads it as a check on a tendency our Lord saw in the disciples, to sit in judgment on the sins of others; they were in danger of a fault hardly less fatal than selfish luxury, the temper of unforgiving judgment, and when they met a case of worldliness they did what we do, condemning without rebuking — whereas friendly reproof aiming at restoration is the truest path to the very forgiveness it seems incompatible with. John Gill turns the words on the hearer both ways, that we neither give offence nor take it, and take heed to our spirits, doctrine and walk; John Wesley says the same in a line. Albert Barnes describes the rebuke practically, as telling a man his fault and the effect of his conduct on your feelings, so that he may acknowledge his error and repent. A.T. Robertson adds only that the verb is an ingressive aorist in a third-class condition.

John Lightfoot sets the precept against rabbinic practice and finds the balance reversed: the rabbis allowed a hundred rebukes if need were and made it a disciple’s duty to rebuke his master, but were sparing about pardon, teaching from strained readings of the prophets that a man is not bound to forgive a fourth trespass.

Whether pardon is owed to the impenitent is the standing question. Bede is careful that our Lord bids us forgive not every man who sins but the man who repents. John Gill presses the same test, that the offender must not merely profess concern but give reason to believe he is heartily grieved and will behave better. John Wesley keeps both halves: this forgiveness is due only to real penitents, and such a man is received as if he had never sinned; but in a lower sense we forgive all, penitent or impenitent, bearing them the sincerest good will and doing them all the good we can, and that not seven times but seventy times seven. Charles Ellicott comes at it from the offender’s side: no accumulation of offences may be allowed to bring us to the hardness that refuses to forgive when the man says he repents.

The number is read three ways. Bede holds that by seven he assigns no bound to pardon but commands us either to forgive all sins or always to forgive the penitent, since seven frequently stands for the whole of a thing or a time. Ambrose derives it from the seventh day on which God rested, after which everlasting rest is promised, so that as the evil works of this world cease the sharpness of punishment may be abated. Charles Ellicott and A.T. Robertson treat it as arithmetic, not symbol: seven times within a single day, which makes the standard the same as the seventy times seven elsewhere, and hard enough for one offender. Ellicott adds that the better manuscripts omit “against thee,” making the command more general.
5:
Theophylact has the disciples hearing of arduous duties, poverty and the avoiding of offences, and asking an increase of faith so as to follow poverty, since nothing so prompts to it as hope in the Lord. John Gill makes them conscious of their weakness, afraid of being stumbled and of giving offence, sensible how hard it is to master resentment and how much they needed fresh grace. John Wesley keeps to the point, that they might thus forgive and neither offend nor be offended, and Albert Barnes that without extraordinary faith they could never keep such a command, though some refer the saying to the failure in the other Gospel. Charles Ellicott reads the fragment as a late addition to the collection of the Lord’s words, noting the exceptional “apostles” for “disciples,” yet finds a sequence: unlimited forgiveness strained their faith too far, and they came with the prayer of many a weak disciple since, like the man who cried, help thou mine unbelief.

Whether the prayer was a good one divides them sharply. Theophylact takes it well, as asking that a faith already begun should increase toward perfection. Charles Ellicott observes that our Lord meets it with what sounds like a reproof, and thinks it needed: the most elementary faith should have taught them that God is love and would help them, so something rang false in it, an unreal diffidence asking as a gift what comes only through active obedience. A.T. Robertson is blunter, that the petition sounds like a stereotyped one from church prayers and that a little reflection shows they should have answered it themselves.

The mustard seed turns on disproportion. Chrysostom takes it as small in size but mightier in power than all other seeds, so that the least faith can do great things; and he defends the apostles, who never transplanted a mulberry — our Lord said not that they should but that they should be able to, and they had no need, doing greater things. He answers an objection from the epistles too: where Paul ascribes the moving of mountains to all faith he does not mean only the whole of faith could do it, but speaks of what seemed great to carnal men. Bede makes it a comparison of appearance and heart, the seed lowly to look at but fervid within, and reads the blood-red mulberry as the Gospel of the cross, uprooted by preaching from the Jewish stock and planted in the Gentile sea. Cyril of Jerusalem presses the disproportion further: the grain is small but fiery in operation, and sown in a little space throws out great branches able to shelter the birds; so faith in the swiftest moment works the greatest effects, the enlightened soul beholding the judgment before the world ends. John Lightfoot shows the comparison to have been common, as a seed, a grain, or a drop of mustard, and suggests the disciples may have been asking for a rule about the measure of faith as they had one about the measure of charity.

The tree itself is a botanical question. Albert Barnes denies that it is the tree we call by that name, reports the mulberry of the old versions, and describes a Palestinian tree of mulberry appearance bearing small greenish figs on short stems along the trunk, eaten only by the poorer sort. Adam Clarke agrees that they stood by such a tree and identifies it with the Egyptian fig, called the mulberry fig from its leaves and fruit. A.T. Robertson observes that both the black and white mulberry grow there, that Luke alone in the New Testament uses either word, and that since the late medical writers keep the distinction though the Septuagint does not, Luke as a physician may be making it deliberately. Charles Ellicott notes that the tree stands where the parallel has the mountain, John Wesley that the saying seems proverbial.
7:
What the parable aims at comes first. Theophylact makes it pride: since faith makes its possessor a keeper of the commandments and adorns him with wonderful works, he might fall into boasting, so the Lord forewarns the apostles by a fit example. Cyril puts the cure more sharply: why boast, when if you do not pay your debt danger is at hand and if you pay it you have done nothing thank-worthy? Charles Ellicott finds a more particular target, the self-righteousness creeping into disciples who asked what they should have; the parable answers their request, since they looked for the crown of labour before the work was done. John Calvin states it flatly: God claims all that is ours as his property and has entire control of our persons and services, so no zeal of ours can lay him under obligation, and being his property we can never be his creditors. Augustine alone denies that the connection is about pride, and takes the passage to answer the petition by a change from faith to faith — from the faith by which we serve God to that by which we enjoy him.

The household details are read literally, then allegorically. Adam Clarke observes that a master never waits on his servant nor owes him thanks, being bound only by the agreed reward, and John Calvin insists the picture is of the ancient slave, not the modern hireling. John Lightfoot supplies a rabbinic counter-instance: the wise men of old gave servants something of all they ate, which was no more than duty, but also made beasts and servants eat first, which he calls supererogation. Augustine takes the field for this life, where a man follows his worldly business or serves foolish men as one tends cattle, and must after his labours return home to the perfect peace of the everlasting kingdom. Bede brings it inside the teacher: the servant leaves the field when a preacher retires for a time into his conscience to weigh his words and deeds, and the supper he makes ready is self-examination after public discourse, with which our Lord desires to be fed. Ambrose draws the plainer moral, that no one sits down before he has passed over, and the Lord does not accept one piece of work only, since as long as we live we ought to be working. Charles Ellicott sets the demand beside the promise at Luke 12:37, where the Master girds himself and ministers to his servants.

What the closing word concedes divides them. Adam Clarke insists that the text says unprofitable, not sinful, since otherwise it would convict the ministering angels too, none of whom can work beyond the powers God has given. Albert Barnes lists four senses: our services do not profit God, the grace to do his will is his own, all we do is duty, and our best service is mingled with imperfection. John Calvin narrows the question: not whether we are justified by works, but whether keeping the law merits reward — and answers no, since God holds us for slaves. Charles Ellicott notes that the same word describes the servant in the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:30), and takes the confession to exclude all boasting, and still more any theory of supererogation or transferred merit. A.T. Robertson renders it useless, and adds that a slavish spirit gains no promotion in business or in the kingdom of God. John Wesley turns it round: a man cannot profit God, and happy is he who judges himself unprofitable; yet our serving him is not unprofitable to us, since he is pleased to give our works a value which by his promise entitles us to an eternal reward. John Gill applies it to ministers and private believers alike, who should be as laborious as the ploughman and the shepherd, one work taken up as another is laid down.
11:
The route is a puzzle because of the order of the names. John Lightfoot raises it: had the text said Galilee and Samaria there would be no difficulty, and as it stands he wonders whether Galilee means Perea, noting that the Syriac and Arabic render the phrase “between,” putting Jesus on the brink of each country for a good way. Albert Barnes agrees, that he passed on the borders of each toward the Jordan, the more probable since otherwise Galilee would have been named first. Adam Clarke keeps the plain order, Galilee then Samaria, since all who went from Galilee to Jerusalem had to pass through it unless they went far about westward. A.T. Robertson notes the only New Testament instance of this preposition with the accusative meaning “through,” and has him going north through both districts to cross the Jordan and join the caravan through Perea; the Samaritans minded northward travellers far less than southward ones. Charles Ellicott marks the first distinct note of time since the ninth chapter, thinks our Lord took neither usual caravan road but one of his own, and observes that the detail, peculiar to Luke, is reported for the sake of the miracle.

Titus Bost makes the ground the point: there was enmity between Jew and Samaritan, and he passed into the midst of both to cement them into one new man, the Samaritans being well disposed toward such mercies and the Jews not. John Gill places the journey at the last passover, and Ambrose connects it back, that after the parable our Lord censures the ungrateful, and John Calvin makes that the object of the narrative: it describes the base ingratitude of the Jewish nation, which is why so many of Christ’s favours were suppressed among them, one man only, a Samaritan, acknowledging his obligation. Matthew Henry notes that leprosy was taken for the punishment of some particular sin, so Christ, who came to take away sin, was at pains to cleanse lepers; he was in the frontier country where he had least acquaintance, and went that road to find them, being found of them that sought him not.

Why they stood at a distance is answered from law and from feeling. Albert Barnes and Adam Clarke cite the statute that shut lepers out from the healthy; Charles Ellicott guesses they kept the legal limit of a hundred paces, with none of the running and falling at his feet of the earlier healing. Theophylact gives the inward reason, that they stood off as ashamed of an uncleanness they supposed Christ would loathe as others did — yet standing afar off they were made nigh by prayer, for the Lord is nigh to all that call upon him in truth. Titus Bost has them waiting for him, drawn together by a common calamity, and contrasts the Jewish law, which counts the outward leprosy unclean, with the Gospel, which counts the inward. John Lightfoot answers the difficulty of ten keeping company: a leper was to dwell alone, but lepers might be with lepers, only different defilements being forbidden to mix — as Charles Ellicott illustrates from the four lepers of 2 Kings 7:3.

Cyril reads the miracle as the Saviour manifesting his glory to draw Israel to the faith, the law that banished them having also prescribed a sacrifice for their purification; Theophylact adds that in sending them to the priests he meant only that they were about to be healed. Augustine takes the lepers mystically for men who profess erroneous doctrines and brazen out their ignorance as wisdom: since leprosy is a blemish of colour, truth mixed with falsehood streaks and disfigures the form, and such men must be put so far from the Church that they may call on Christ with loud shouts — their calling him Teacher implying that this leprosy is false doctrine a teacher can wash away.
13:
John Gill has them lifting their voices together and crying aloud because they were at a distance and their desire was vehement. Adam Clarke makes more of the singleness: though ten cried at once there was but one voice among them, companions in suffering being companions in prayer — whence his rule that prayer should be strong and earnest when the disease is great and inveterate, sin being the worst of leprosies. Charles Ellicott notes that their title is the evangelist’s usual equivalent for Rabbi, and supposes an earlier cleansing of a leper had come to their knowledge somehow.

How much faith the ten had is the first substantial question. John Calvin argues from their obedience: they would never have set out but for faith, since it would be absurd to present themselves to the judges of leprosy to attest a cure if Christ’s promise were worth no more than an inspection — they bore a visible leprosy and yet on his bare word made no scruple of declaring themselves clean, so some seed of faith must have been implanted, though he adds that they were not therefore regenerated by the Spirit of adoption. Albert Barnes makes the same point from the order of events, that he did not heal them first and then send them, so that the command carried only an implied assurance and required no small measure of faith. Charles Ellicott sharpens it by comparison, that here there was no accompanying touch as an outward means and pledge of healing, so the command was a greater trial of faith than it had been before. Adam Clarke presses it into a maxim: they had no promise and went at his bare command to do what only healed men were required to do, and God highly honours such faith, whereas he who will not believe till he has what he calls a reason is never likely to be saved, the highest reason for believing being that God has commanded it. Albert Barnes turns it into an appeal, that sinners defiled with the leprosy of sin should trust the Lord Jesus and obey his directions, and shall in due time have the evidence that their peace is made.

What the sending to the priests was for divides them along familiar lines. John Calvin holds that the reply was equivalent to saying, you are clean, since the discernment of leprosy belonged by law to the priests (Leviticus 14:2); Christ preserves their right entire and appeals to them as witnesses who must approve the miracle he had wrought. He then turns the passage against those who build auricular confession on it: they were sent not to pour their sins into a priest’s ears but to offer the sacrifice the law enjoined, and not to be made clean but because they were clean already. Albert Barnes gives the civil reason, that the inspection was how a man obtained leave to mingle again in society, and that the journey was to exhibit the evidence of a cure. Charles Ellicott removes a practical difficulty, that the command implied no journey to Jerusalem, any priest in any town being qualified to pronounce on the cure; and he leaves open whether the taint went suddenly or by degrees. Adam Clarke keeps to the paradox of the order, that they were sent to do what belonged only to the healed while they were still unhealed, and A.T. Robertson notes that the phrase for their going is a favourite construction of this evangelist.
15:
When the man turned back is a small chronological question with a moral edge. Adam Clarke takes it at its plainest, that he did not wait to go first to the priest but turned immediately and gave public praise to the hand from which he had received his cure. Charles Ellicott reads the wording to mean that the healing was not complete until the company was at least out of sight. John Calvin canvasses both possibilities and prefers the less obvious: Luke’s words seem to suggest a return halfway, but he thinks it more probable that the man went on, heard the priests’ decision and then came back, since he needed their leave before returning to ordinary intercourse and had no right to neglect Christ’s command or to defraud the temple of its sacrifice — though he allows the other conjecture, that a devout zeal seized him the moment he saw himself clean, so that he began his sacrifice with thanksgiving. Albert Barnes reaches a similar reconciliation from the other end: there is no evidence that he failed to go to the priest afterwards, since he could not otherwise have been restored to society, but he poured out his thanks first.

What the order of his actions teaches is pressed hard. Albert Barnes makes it a pattern, that the first duty of sinners who have been forgiven and have the hope of eternal life is to prostrate themselves at the feet of their great Benefactor and consecrate themselves to his service, and only then to go and show others the evidence, mingling like a restored leper with family and friends and proving by the purity of their lives how great the mercy was. John Gill notes what made the evidence unmistakable, that the man felt soundness in his body and saw with his eyes that the leprosy was gone; and on the prostration he observes that being cleansed he might now draw near, which he did with profound reverence and a deep sense of the favour received.

That the grateful man was a Samaritan is where every commentator stops. Adam Clarke makes the contrast one of religion, that he professed a very corrupt one and less was to be expected of him than of the other nine, who were probably Jews. Albert Barnes makes it one of reputation, since the Jews considered the Samaritans peculiarly wicked and themselves peculiarly holy, so that the incident, like the parable of the good Samaritan, was designed to break that down. A.T. Robertson says the touch colours the whole incident and notes that the pronoun has point: the one man grateful enough to return was a despised Samaritan. Charles Ellicott reads it as part of the evangelist’s purpose throughout, the breaking down of every middle wall of partition, and supposes that a narrative peculiar to this Gospel came to him in the course of his own inquiries in Galilee and Samaria; he adds the sadder observation that the barrier had already been broken down for a time by the common pressure of calamity without any enduring sense of fellowship taking its place, since the nine seem to have separated from the Samaritan as soon as they were cleansed — men want more than shared misery before they learn brotherhood.

John Calvin turns the words that follow into a national charge, that Christ is expostulating with the whole people by the comparison of one stranger with many Jews, whose custom it was to swallow God’s favours without any feeling of piety — which is why miracles so numerous and so splendid gained him hardly any reputation among them; and he warns that the same complaint is brought generally against all of us if we do not at least repay divine favours with the duty of gratitude.
17:
The question about the nine is heard as a reproach with a wide reach. Charles Ellicott finds a tone of mingled surprise, grief and indignation, and raises the ethical difficulty squarely: if the nine had faith enough to be healed — and the healing proves they had — how did it not show itself further in gratitude and love? His answer comes from the analogous case in the spiritual life, where men have the faith that justifies, are pardoned, and feel the burden lifted, yet show no glow of loving gratitude and shrink from fellowship with others divided from them by outward lines of demarcation; he instances the Baptist’s disciples who kept a separatist life at Ephesus without the warmth of the indwelling Spirit, and adds that most churches supply many more. Albert Barnes generalises to deliverance of every kind: when men are recovered from danger or saved from a wreck, one here and there acknowledges the goodness of God while the mass give no thanks and go back to their employments. Adam Clarke turns it on converts instead: where are the numbers converted from time to time, and are they still praising him with their faces in the dust as they did at first, or have they mingled again with the world? John Gill keeps to the wording, that it does not appear any of them had returned.

The word for the man who did return is examined closely. Charles Ellicott notes that it means a man of another race, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament though the Greek Old Testament has it, and was probably a term of contempt implying that Samaritans were no children of Abraham. A.T. Robertson supplies a parallel: the same word stands on the stone from the temple enclosure forbidding any foreigner to pass within the screen about the sanctuary — an inscription Jesus may have read. Adam Clarke draws the moral from the fact rather than the word: God often receives more praise and more affectionate obedience from men who long lived without knowledge of him than from those bred up among his people, for the plain reason that those who have much forgiven will love much.

What the closing sentence grants him is the last question, and it divides sharply. Adam Clarke keeps it to the cure, that faith was the means by which he received the influence that cleansed him. Charles Ellicott takes the verb to carry both its senses at once, since the same word is elsewhere rendered that his faith had saved him: the nine had faith sufficient for the health of the body, while this man’s had gone further and given a new and purer life to his soul. John Calvin reaches the same by argument. Some restrict the word to cleanness of the flesh, but then, since Christ commends this man’s lively faith, how did the other nine obtain the same bodily cure? We must conclude that Christ pronounces an estimate of God’s gift quite unlike the one ungodly men pronounce: it was a token and pledge of fatherly love. The ungrateful efface the remembrance of grace, so the cure is debased by their ingratitude and yields them none of its advantage, whereas faith alone sanctifies God’s gifts and turns their lawful use toward salvation — from which he infers that the soul’s eternal salvation was included with the temporal gift. Albert Barnes ends practically, that the dismissal sends him to the priest after all, since without that certificate he could not rejoin society or public worship: gratitude expressed, he is to go and obey the law of God, as renewed sinners still should.
20:
The spirit of the question is weighed first. Cyril hears open derision, as though they said that before the kingdom he talked of came, the death of the cross would be his lot; and being reviled he reviled not again. John Calvin agrees it was mockery, since Christ kept speaking of a kingdom at hand while nothing changed in the outward condition of the Jews, which gave malicious men an excuse for harassing him; he allows that others may trace the question to grossness of view rather than jeering, and thinks Christ disregards the mockers and shapes his reply for the disciples. Charles Ellicott finds two sets of questioners, the taunt of the hostile and something like impatience in the rest, the answer meeting both. Matthew Henry gives the expectation behind it, a temporal kingdom that should advance the Jewish nation above the nations.

What is denied by “not with observation” is defined narrowly. Charles Ellicott renders it careful and anxious watching, with a special force, since some Pharisees had watched Christ with hostile purpose while others looked for a sign from heaven; neither watching would catch the kingdom, which would burst on them suddenly. A.T. Robertson traces the term through its technical uses, medical writers watching symptoms and astronomers their close observations, and concludes that no such scrutiny of externals will reveal the signs of the kingdom. John Calvin takes the word for extraordinary splendour, some great display such that every man might take notice, and John Wesley for outward pomp that draws everyone’s eye. John Lightfoot distinguishes two scriptural senses of the kingdom of God: in some places the propagation of the gospel by the Messiah and his followers, especially among the Gentiles, in others his victory and vengeance upon the Jews who opposed it.

The denial of a place is illustrated from the manner of princes and of pretenders. Albert Barnes observes that an earthly prince visiting his territories attracts notice, so that where he is and which way he goes becomes important news; the Messiah would come with no such pomp but silently and obscurely. He adds that the words may glance at the pretenders who promised signs in this mountain or that desert. Adam Clarke supplies a third conjecture, that the Pharisees may have supposed the Messiah kept secret in some private place known only to their rulers, to be produced in due time as Joash was by the priest (2 Chronicles 23:1). John Gill keeps to the words, that no one shall be able to point and say it is here or there.

Whether the kingdom is within them or among them is the standing dispute. Charles Ellicott holds that the marginal “among you” has been adopted somewhat hastily: on that reading the words assert the kingdom’s presence among the very men asking when it would appear, but the preposition is all but decisive against it, being used of what is within as against what is without, as in the inside of the cup at Matthew 23:26; it is in that region, the life which must be born again, that men were to look. A.T. Robertson reaches the same more sharply: the examples cited from the classical writers for “among” do not bear investigation, so what Jesus tells the Pharisees is that they, like others, must look for the kingdom within themselves and not in outward displays. Albert Barnes leaves both open, either that the reign of God is in the heart, setting up its dominion over the passions rather than merely controlling external actions, or that the new dispensation is already among them. John Wesley keeps both, that it is now in the midst of them and present in the soul of every true believer, a spiritual kingdom which wherever it exists exists in the heart.
22:
Whose desire is meant divides the entry. Cyril reads the words as preparation for suffering: before the coming from heaven at the end of the world, persecution will break out on the disciples so terribly that they will wish back one of the days when they still walked with Christ. John Wesley puts it briefly, one day of mercy, or one day of such converse as they had then. Albert Barnes turns it forward, to the vengeance about to fall on the Jewish nation: calamities so heavy that the disciples would greatly desire a deliverer, the Son of man meaning the Messiah without asserting who he was. Charles Ellicott keeps both directions at once, the backward glance of regret and the forward look of yearning — the first foretold when the children of the bride-chamber were told they should fast once the Bridegroom was taken, the second heard later in the cry of the souls beneath the altar; and he insists that the disciples, not the Pharisees, are addressed, so that in the weary years of conflict they would often wish themselves back in the Galilean converse or carried on to the final victory. John Gill reports a further suggestion, that the disciples might through pity desire the removal of punishments that could not be removed, but thinks the other sense likelier.

The warning against places is text and prudence together. John Gill notes that some copies add the name of Christ, so the cry runs that Christ is in such a place and will quickly deliver the nation from the Romans, and Adam Clarke confirms the addition from a body of manuscripts, calling it undoubtedly the meaning. Albert Barnes supplies the history, that many false Christs appeared about that time and tried to lead the people away. A.T. Robertson reads the prohibition as ingressive and turns it into advice: do not rush after men who set times and places for the second advent, since the Messiah was already present in the first, though the Pharisees did not know it. John Wesley catches the error in a phrase: such men limit his presence to this or that place. Charles Ellicott notes that the words are all but identical with the parallel, the difference of context being another instance of the same language recurring on a fresh occasion.

The lightning shows the manner of the coming. Charles Ellicott observes a variation from the parallel, the two parts under heaven standing where the other has east and west, and the day of the Son of man where the other has the formal word for his coming. A.T. Robertson draws the consequence, that the coming will be sudden and universally visible, and adds that there are still poor souls waiting in Jerusalem under the delusion that Jesus will come there and nowhere else. John Wesley says the appearing will be as swift and as wide as the flash. Bede presses the detail about the part under heaven, since the judgment will be given in the midst of the air, where we shall be caught up in the clouds; and if the Lord appears like lightning, no man stays hidden in the deep of his heart, for the brightness of the Judge pierces through him.

The interposed prophecy of the Passion is noticed by all. A.T. Robertson states the logic in a line, that the second coming will be only after the Cross. Adam Clarke makes it causal, that the desolation cannot come until the cup of that people’s iniquity is full by their crucifying the Lord of glory. Charles Ellicott treats the interposition as significant, an individualising feature of this record that a prophecy of the Passion should sit inside a discourse on the second advent. John Gill lists what the suffering included, the mockings and spitting and scourging that must come before he entered his glory.
26:
Bede marks the change of figure, the coming just compared to lightning being now likened to the days of Noah and of Lot, when sudden destruction came on mankind; the catena adds, under a hand it does not separate out, that their unbelief proceeded from self-indulgence and softness of mind, since as a man’s wishes are, so will his expectations be. Eusebius explains the second example: having used the deluge, our Lord cites Lot so that none should look for another destruction by water, the wrath of God being now to descend by fire. Charles Ellicott notes that here again the days of the Son of man stand where the formal word for his coming stands elsewhere, and John Wesley defines them as those which immediately follow the day eminently so called.

What exactly was charged against that generation is answered with care. John Gill denies that eating and drinking with moderation is blameworthy or inconsistent with religious exercises, and finds the fault in an extravagant living that put far off the evil day Noah told them of. Ambrose guards the same ground: marriage and meat and drink are not condemned, since by the one succession is sustained and by the other nature; what is asked is moderation, whatever exceeds it being of evil. Bede makes the mildness of the charge the point: passing by the unutterable wickedness of the Sodomites, our Lord names only what might be thought trifling offences, so that we may see how fearfully unlawful pleasures are punished when lawful ones taken to excess are repaid with fire and brimstone. Adam Clarke puts it as an account of a whole life rather than of particular acts: they lived wholly for this world and made no provision for their souls, and the same carelessness met the Romans coming against Judea, no one regarding the warnings given by the Son of God. Ambrose adds the deeper cause, that the deluge was brought on by our sins, since God did not create evil and our own deservings found it out for themselves.

The two examples are read for a rule about timing. Bede observes that the fire did not fall on Sodom till Lot had gone out, as the flood did not come till Noah had entered: while the righteous dwelt among the wicked God suspended his anger lest they perish together, and when he meant to destroy he first withdrew them — so at the end of the world the consummation will not come before the just are separated. He also reads the ark mystically, as the Lord building his Church out of faithful servants joined like smooth pieces of wood, entering it when finished as at the day of judgment he who always dwells within will enlighten it with his visible presence; while the ark is building the wicked flourish, and once it is entered they perish.

The grammar is made to carry part of the argument. Charles Ellicott prefers a rendering that keeps the tense, that they were eating and drinking and marrying, the form implying continuous and repeated action; and he notes that the Greek word for the flood is used in the New Testament only of Noah’s deluge, the sense having been stamped on it by the Greek Old Testament. A.T. Robertson presses the same contrast: the verbs of ordinary life stand in the imperfect, vividly picturing the manner of that time, while the decisive acts — that Noah entered, that the flood came, that it destroyed them — all stand in the aorist. John Gill places the whole scene in the years while the ark was building and before Noah went into it.
28:
The second example is peculiar to this Gospel, and Charles Ellicott accounts for it: the illustration is absent from the otherwise parallel passage, but was naturally suggested by our Lord’s frequent references to the cities of the plain, and the later allusion to Lot at 2 Peter 2:7 may perhaps be traced to the impression this revival of the history made on the apostle who heard it. He notes the tense again, that they were buying and selling rather than simply bought and sold, and finds a characteristic difference in the particular verbs chosen here, since buying, selling, planting and building mark a higher advance in social life than the eating and marrying of Noah’s day. A.T. Robertson makes the same grammatical point structurally, that the ordinary occupations all stand in the imperfect while the acts of the following verse — that Lot went out, that it rained, that it destroyed them — all stand in the aorist.

How the overthrow was accomplished is where the entry divides. Albert Barnes argues for natural means directed by God: he is not to be supposed to have created fire and brimstone for the occasion, any more than he created the waters to drown the world, since there he merely broke up the fountains of the great deep and opened the windows of heaven. He fills in the local detail, that the four cities stood on a plain where the Dead Sea now lies, on ground abounding as that region still does in bitumen, which is easily kindled and burns with great intensity, and adds that the phrase for fire and brimstone is a Hebrew form denoting sulphurous fire. Adam Clarke works from the Hebrew of the original narrative in the other direction, arguing that a subject should be supplied to the verb, since it is there said that Jehovah rained fire and brimstone from Jehovah out of heaven. Charles Ellicott keeps to the words themselves, that the pairing of the two Greek terms comes from the Greek version of Genesis 19:24 and plainly suggested the same combination in the Revelation. John Gill supplies the timing from the narrative and from Jewish tradition, that Lot was plucked out early, with the sun risen as he reached Zoar, and that the day is reckoned the sixteenth of Nisan.

Which revelation is meant is the last question. John Gill takes both at once, the coming in power to avenge himself on the Jews and the revealing from heaven in flaming fire at the last day; the parallel holds at every point, since men lived in carnality and security in the days of Noah and Lot, the Jews buoyed themselves up with hopes of deliverance to the last, and such will be the times of indolence and supineness before the day of judgment. He carries the comparison through the suddenness, that as those destructions came unexpectedly so did the fall of Jerusalem and so will the burning of the world, and through the remnant, since as Noah was saved in the ark and Lot snatched out of Sodom, so the Christians withdrew from Jerusalem to Pella. Albert Barnes keeps to the nearer event, that destruction came on the old world and on Sodom suddenly, while men were engaged in other things and little expecting it, and so suddenly it would come upon the Jewish people. A.T. Robertson reads the verb as a prophetic and futuristic present, which throws the weight the other way.
31:
What day is meant is settled first. John Gill and John Wesley both refer it to the approach of the Roman armies against Jerusalem, Wesley adding that this event will be the grand type of the last day. Theophylact notes that the other Gospel places it all at the destruction of the city, when those on the housetop were not to come down nor those in the field to turn home; so it happened at the taking of Jerusalem, will happen at the coming of Antichrist, and most of all at the completion of all things. Eusebius narrows it to the last of these, taking the day for the time before the end of the world and the danger for a persecution from the son of perdition, in which the man who is fleeing must not turn back for his goods lest he imitate Lot’s wife. A.T. Robertson declines the local reading and takes the application to be an absolute indifference to worldly interests as the attitude of readiness for the Son of man, noting an unusual imperative where the ordinary idiom would take the subjunctive. Charles Ellicott corrects only the old rendering of the noun, which means his goods.

The Latin reading is quite different. Ambrose begins from the affliction of good men, vexed in this world on account of the wicked so that they may receive a fuller reward in the next, and reads the housetop as the summit of the highest virtues: a man who has climbed there must not fall back to the grovelling business of this world. The block continues, under a hand the scrape has not separated, with the same figure worked further — the man on the housetop is one who has departed from carnal things and breathes the free air of a spiritual life, while the vessels left in the house are the carnal senses, which many have used to discover a truth that only the intellect can take in, and so have missed it altogether.

Lot’s wife draws a warning about the manner of flight rather than its direction. Albert Barnes makes the fault delay rather than curiosity: she looked back and lingered, perhaps wishing to carry something away, so the disciples are charged not to look back nor delay but to escape quickly, remembering that by delaying she lost her life. Adam Clarke agrees that she probably turned back to save some of her goods, as the preceding verse seems to intimate, and draws the sharper moral that it is a proof of criminal affection when we leave with grief and anxiety what the Lord has commanded us to abandon. A.T. Robertson warns in the same terms against looking back with yearning after what has been left behind. John Wesley reduces it to a rule of speed, to escape without ever looking behind. Charles Ellicott observes that the reference, like the use of Lot generally, is peculiar to this Gospel and speaks for its independence, and notes that the history had already been used to point a like moral, the standing pillar of salt having become a monument of an unbelieving soul.

John Gill collects what the Jewish writers say of her: they give her a name and make her a native of Sodom, and explain the backward look either as a wish to see the end of her father’s house or as a mother’s heart yearning after the daughters she had left. He follows the tradition into natural history too, that the salt of Sodom was reckoned hard as a stone, that a Galilean salt of like hardness was known, and that elsewhere salt was quarried and used to build houses and walls — a substance of very durable nature.
33:
The saying about losing life to keep it is examined for its verbs. Charles Ellicott notes that the better manuscripts give a word rendered elsewhere as purchase, suggesting a transaction where the ordinary word for saving does not: a man buys his lower life at the price of the higher and is a loser by the bargain. A.T. Robertson takes the second verb, which means to bring forth alive and so to keep alive, and remarks that it is a late word common in the medical writers. John Gill gives the concrete sense for that generation, of a man who tries to save himself by fleeing to a stronghold or staying in the strongest city of the nation. John Wesley paraphrases: however great the danger, do not seek to save your life by violating conscience, for you will surely lose it, whereas losing it for his sake is repaid with life everlasting — and the likeliest way to preserve it now is to be always ready to give it up, a peculiar providence then putting a difference between you and other men. Adam Clarke and Albert Barnes both note that the same or similar words were spoken on other occasions.

The night and the pairs are read at three levels. John Gill takes the night for the calamity coming on the Jewish nation and warns against understanding it literally, and A.T. Robertson makes the demonstrative more vivid still, on this night, when Christ comes. Ambrose hears something else: night is well said, because Antichrist is the hour of darkness and pours a cloud over men’s minds while declaring himself to be Christ, whereas Christ shines like lightning, so that in that night we may see the glory of the resurrection. He also draws the moral from the division itself, that God is not unjust in separating men of like pursuits who differ in quality. Bede connects the pairs to the warning just given: the man in the field was told not to turn back, and lest that seem to touch only those who openly return and publicly deny their Lord, he goes on to show that some seem to keep their face forward and are yet looking behind in heart.

Augustine works the three pairs into a scheme of classes. The first is of men who prefer their ease and quiet and busy themselves with neither secular nor ecclesiastical concerns, whose quiet life the bed signifies; the second is of those placed among the people and governed by teachers, described as women because it is best for them to be ruled by the advice of those set over them, and as grinding at the mill because in their hands revolves the wheel of temporal concerns, and as grinding together because they serve the benefit of the Church; the third is of those who labour in the ministry as in the field of God. In each of the three there are two sorts of men, the one abiding in the Church and taken up, the other falling away and left behind.

The catena attaches the comment on the eagles here as well. Eusebius offers two readings: that the birds feeding on dead animals are the rulers of the world who will persecute the saints, in whose power are left all unworthy of being taken up and called the carcass; or that they are the avenging powers which fly about to torment the wicked. Adam Clarke ends on a textual note, holding without doubt that the verse about two men in the field is an interpolation borrowed from the parallel: it is wanting in a long list of manuscripts and versions and in many of the fathers, the editors leave it out, and the old translators marked in the margin that it is missing from most Greek copies.
35:
The last pairs are read at the plainest level by John Gill, who takes the two women at the mill and the two men in the field for people at their ordinary work — tilling, sowing or reaping, whichever the season required — at the hour when Jerusalem fell. Cyril of Jerusalem is the one voice who hears the anxiety such a division must raise, and answers it directly. He puts the objections into the mouths of his hearers: I am a poor man; I shall perhaps be found sick in bed at that time; I am but a woman, and shall be taken at the mill — are we then to be despised? His reply is that the Judge is no respecter of persons and will not judge by a man’s appearance nor reprove according to his speech, honouring neither the learned before the simple nor the rich before the needy. Though you be in the field, he says, the angels shall take you, and do not imagine that he will take the landowners and leave you the husbandman; though you be a slave or poor, be not in the least distressed, for he who took the form of a servant does not despise servants; though you lie sick in bed, it is written that two shall be in one bed and the one taken; and though you be put by compulsion to grind, man or woman, and sit in fetters beside the mill, he who by his might brings out the prisoners is not hindered.

The question that follows is understood in more than one way. John Gill is careful about its object: the disciples, to whom the discourse was chiefly directed, do not ask where the abandoned will be left but whither the others will be taken, and by whom. Albert Barnes takes it instead as a question of direction, where or in what quarter these calamities would fall. Charles Ellicott notices that the question fits this place, where the future had been foreshadowed in parables and dark sayings, and would not have been natural in the parallel account, where the whole context had already fixed the locality our Lord was speaking of; he adds that the only variation in the reply is the use of body for carcase.

The reply is treated as a proverb with a rule inside it. Albert Barnes reads it as pointing to guilt: eagles flock where there is prey, so the armies will gather where the wickedness is greatest, and by that answer the disciples’ thoughts were directed at once to Jerusalem as the place where the calamities might be expected to begin. Adam Clarke makes the same inference but leaves the application to the hearer, since our Lord answers in a figure they must work out for themselves: where the sin is, there will the punishment be. He adds a naturalist’s observation in support, that the jackal and the vulture are devourers of dead bodies and that it is very remarkable how suddenly such birds appear after a death in the open field, though not one may have been seen in the place for a long time before. A.T. Robertson agrees that the birds are more probably vultures attracted by the carcass than eagles, notes that the proverb is quoted in the parallel discourse as well, and observes that the double compound of the verb completes the picture of a gathering from every quarter. Charles Ellicott generalises furthest: the repetition of a half-proverbial saying at a later period shows its importance as a law of God’s government, for men ask where his judgments fall and the answer is that they fall wherever they are needed.
